record.file_problem: Partial: this is a LessWrong summary of a linked paper, not the full paper. The referenced figures and the details in the cited sections are not included.
record.tranche_reason: Reports grokking in linear regression and Gaussian-process models, extending the phenomenon to model classes beyond neural networks, and reports a data-augmentation experiment on algorithmic datasets.
record.gate_note: The post summarizes the authors’ own findings. It gives qualitative outcomes but omits the underlying figures and most experimental details. It also mentions related work as inspiration; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The post reports the authors' own observations of delayed generalization in non-neural models (GP classification on parity, GP regression, linear regression). It also reports a neural-network experiment on algorithmic data where appended noise dimensions lengthen the train-to-validation gap. It adds trajectory analyses offered as support for a regularization-driven complexity account. All evidence is qualitative: the post is a summary without figures or numbers.
record.authors_conclusion: Largely correct. The authors report grokking in GP classification, GP regression and linear regression, which they say shows it is not specific to SGD or weight-norm regularization. They induce grokking on algorithmic data by adding spurious noise dimensions. They hypothesise that grokking arises when regularization slowly guides solutions from low-error/high-complexity regions to low-error/low-complexity regions. They treat circuit competition as a special case and admit there is no mathematical proof.
record.recipe_differences: The post summarizes experiments on linear regression and Gaussian-process models, plus an algorithmic-data augmentation method; it does not give enough detail to compare the experimental recipe directly with the original.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported interval between high training and validation accuracy varies with the number of added dimensions; the post says this relationship appears to align with exponential regression.

fits_no_version.finding: Delayed generalization is reported in linear regression and GP regression, models without feature learning and without SGD or weight-norm regularization. The tasks are unspecified.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking-like delayed generalization occurs in non-neural model classes (linear regression, GPs), so it does not require feature learning or SGD.

fits_no_version.finding: The authors hypothesise that regularization slowly moves solutions from low-error/high-complexity regions to low-error/low-complexity regions along a non-increasing-loss path.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Grokking is governed by the accessibility of low-complexity, low-error regions in the complexity and error landscapes; circuit competition is a special case.

record.problems: The post is a short summary rather than the full paper; numerical outcomes, experimental settings, and the referenced figure details are absent. The authors state that their theory has no mathematical proof.
record.rows_left_out: No additional result rows were available from the post beyond those recorded; the referenced figures and details from Sections 2.2, 2.3, and Appendix E are not included.

The data types of the regression experiments are not stated; there is no initialization-scale or weight-norm switch.

missing.locator: Full paper arXiv:2310.17247, Sections 2.2, 2.3, Appendix E (not in the post)

record.verdict_notes: The source is a LessWrong summary only, so all evidence is qualitative and no row has readable values. The rows' links to V5 for r1–r3 were removed, because those rows report only that grokking occurs. No V5 verdict is given because r5 and r6 have no readable measure. The authors' argument that grokking does not need weight-norm regularization is compatible with V5's phrase 'or another bias toward low norm', so it is not counted as a challenge.

versions.untested_parts: The post does not report whether shrinking the training set increases the optimization delay.
No gradual formation of a Fourier or other generalizing circuit, removal of memorizing components, or continuous progress measure anticipating an accuracy jump is reported.
The reported non-neural examples are not stated to use non-algorithmic data. No initialization-scale or weight-norm switch is reported.
No LLM pretraining or fine-tuning on realistic data is reported.
The post discusses complexity, error, and regularization, but does not report a direct test of low-norm preference, a critical dataset size, or ungrokking below that size.
No comparison of whether separate runs converge to the same identifiable algorithm is reported.
No adaptive-optimizer instability or floating-point/softmax artifact control is reported.
